analysis.investment_thesis: MedPlus is a decent pharmacy roll-up business priced as a high-quality compounder — at 50x earnings with ROE of only 8.8%, the market is demanding near-perfect execution in an intensely competitive, thin-margin industry where returns barely cover cost of capital. At INR 878, the price reflects years of flawless growth, leaving no margin of safety for the inevitable setbacks in commodity retail.
key_strengths: Strong revenue CAGR of 15.1% over 9 years with EBITDA compounding at 30.9%, showing genuine operating leverage as the store network matures.
FY2025 FCF of INR 482 Cr was a step-change improvement with capex falling to just INR 59 Cr, suggesting the heavy store-rollout phase may be plateauing into cash generation.
Institutional conviction is reasonable — DIIs hold 26.6% and promoters 40.3% — limiting egregious governance risk.
key_risks: Returns are structurally weak: ROCE of 10.3% barely clears India's cost of equity (12–15%), meaning the business at scale is not creating economic value — it is consuming capital at a modest spread.

Intense competitive pressure from Apollo Pharmacy, Tata 1mg, Reliance Netmeds, and aggregators threatens the already razor-thin 4.75% operating margin, with virtually no moat in commodity drug dispensing.

Finance costs of INR 103 Cr consumed 69% of FY2025 net profit (INR 150 Cr); borrowings have grown from INR 477 Cr in FY2020 to INR 1,193 Cr in FY2025, amplifying downside in any margin or growth disappointment.
red_flags: ROE of 8.8% paired with a 50x P/E is a value-destroying combination — the equity is priced as if it earns 20%+ returns, when it earns barely half the cost of capital.

FCF has been wildly volatile over the past five years (-78 in FY2023, +482 in FY2025) — the FY2025 spike is driven largely by capex compression, not a durable improvement in unit economics. One re-acceleration of store openings reverses this.
EV/EBITDA of 28x for a 4.75% operating-margin retailer implies a terminal-value bet with zero tolerance for error — this is a '2 AM optimism' valuation, not a margin-of-safety price.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The central problem with MedPlus is not the business — it is the price. A pharmacy retailer with 4.75% operating margins and 8.8% ROE is fundamentally a low-return, capital-intensive roll-up. The market is pricing it at 50x trailing earnings and 28x EV/EBITDA, multiples appropriate for businesses earning 20–25% returns on capital with durable pricing power. MedPlus earns neither. Debt-to-EBITDA sits at roughly 2.25x (INR 1,193 Cr borrowings / INR 529 Cr EBITDA), manageable today but dangerous if margins compress even 100 bps in a price-war scenario. Free cash flow yield on current market cap is just ~4.6% (INR 482 Cr FCF / INR 10,544 Cr Mcap) — below my minimum 6–8% threshold — and that 482 Cr itself is a one-year anomaly propped up by unusually low capex of INR 59 Cr vs. a normalized INR 100–170 Cr range. Strip that out and the underlying FCF yield is sub-2%.

Second-level thinking demands asking: what does the price already reflect? At 50x earnings, the market has fully priced in sustained 20–25% earnings growth, stable margins, manageable competition, and a successful scale-out of diagnostics and private label. That is a lot of consensus optimism in a sector where Apollo Pharmacy, D-Mart's pharmacy push, and digital-first aggregators are all fighting for the same INR 2 lakh crore Indian pharmacy market. When consensus is uniformly bullish in a thin-margin retail business with rising debt, that is precisely when Howard Marks walks away. The asymmetry is deeply unfavorable: upside is limited without multiple expansion (which is unlikely given where rates and valuations are), while downside in a competitive shock or margin disappointment could easily be 40–50% from current levels. I see no margin of safety here at any reasonable intrinsic value estimate.
